entries.title: Phishing and how to recognize a phishing email
entries.tags: phishing email scam fake link spoof sender recognize spot lure
entries.answer: Phishing is a scam where an attacker pretends to be a trusted organisation to trick you into clicking a link, opening an attachment, or handing over passwords or payment details. Warning signs: urgent or threatening language ('your account will be closed'), a sender address that doesn't match the real domain, links whose real URL (hover to check) points somewhere else, unexpected attachments, requests for credentials or gift cards, and generic greetings. When in doubt, don't click: go to the site yourself or call the organisation using a number you already trust.
entries.more: Spear phishing targets one person using personal details; smishing is phishing by SMS (what this project's SpamShield detector classifies); vishing is by phone. Defences that work together: MFA (so a stolen password isn't enough), a password manager (it won't autofill on a fake domain), email filtering, and reporting suspicious messages so others are warned.

entries.title: Creating a strong password
entries.tags: strong password passphrase create good secure length password manager reuse
entries.answer: A strong password is long, unique, and unpredictable. Use a passphrase of 4 or more random words or at least 14 characters, never reuse it on another site, and avoid personal details like names, birthdays, or pet names. A password manager can generate and remember a different strong password for every account, and you should turn on multi-factor authentication wherever it's offered.
entries.more: Length beats complexity: 'correct-horse-battery-staple' is far harder to crack than 'P@ssw0rd1'. Reuse is the biggest risk, because one breached site lets attackers try the same email and password everywhere (credential stuffing, which the Security Monitor detected in its log). Check haveibeenpwned.com to see if your email appears in known breaches.

entries.title: Denial-of-service (DoS) attack
entries.tags: dos denial of service attack availability flood overload server crash website down
entries.answer: A denial-of-service (DoS) attack tries to make a website or service unavailable to real users by overwhelming it with traffic or requests, or by exploiting a bug that crashes it. It attacks availability, the 'A' in the CIA triad. Examples include HTTP floods, SYN floods that exhaust connection tables, and slow attacks like Slowloris that hold connections open.
entries.more: Defences: rate limiting, a CDN or DDoS-protection service that absorbs traffic, web application firewalls, auto-scaling, and monitoring that alerts on sudden traffic spikes. Assignment 7 on this site analyses real DDoS traffic from the CIC-IDS2017 dataset.

entries.title: Difference between DoS and DDoS attacks
entries.tags: difference dos ddos distributed botnet compare versus vs many sources
entries.answer: A DoS attack comes from a single source, so it can often be stopped by blocking or rate-limiting that one IP. A DDoS (distributed denial-of-service) attack comes from many machines at once, usually a botnet of infected computers or IoT devices, so the combined traffic is much larger and blocking individual IPs doesn't work. Defenders must filter by behaviour instead.
entries.more: In Assignment 7, the DDoS flows in CIC-IDS2017 were individually small and slow; the attack's power came from 128,014 near-identical connections. A simple 'high packets per second' rule caught almost none of them, while a Random Forest using flow shape reached an F1 score of about 99.96%. The Security Monitor shows the same pattern: a flood from 90 IPs detected by a per-minute request-rate z-score.

entries.title: Protecting your computer from malware
entries.tags: malware virus trojan ransomware protect antivirus computer infection worm spyware
entries.answer: To protect against malware: keep your operating system, browser, and apps updated; use built-in antivirus such as Microsoft Defender and keep it on; only install software from official sources; don't open unexpected attachments or enable macros in documents; use a standard (non-admin) account day to day; and keep regular backups, ideally one offline, so ransomware can't hold your files hostage.
entries.more: Malware types: viruses and worms spread themselves, trojans pretend to be useful software, spyware steals information, and ransomware encrypts files and demands payment. Most infections start with phishing or unpatched software, so updates and caution with links stop the majority.

entries.title: SQL injection
entries.tags: sql injection sqli database query input union select quote web attack
entries.answer: SQL injection happens when a website puts user input straight into a database query, so an attacker can type SQL code instead of normal data, for example ' OR '1'='1 in a login box. That can let them bypass logins or read, change, or delete data. The fix is parameterised queries (prepared statements), which keep data separate from code, plus input validation and least-privilege database accounts.
entries.more: The Security Monitor flagged an IP sending 42 SQL injection probes such as /products?id=42 UNION SELECT username,password FROM users--, caught by a signature rule looking for quotes with OR/AND, UNION SELECT, comment markers, and DROP. Signature rules are fast but can miss obfuscated payloads, so the real defence is in the code.

entries.title: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
entries.tags: xss cross site scripting script injection javascript browser cookie
entries.answer: Cross-site scripting (XSS) is when an attacker gets a website to include their JavaScript in a page that other people view. The script runs in the victim's browser and can steal session cookies, change the page, or act as the user. Defences: escape or encode output, validate input, use a Content Security Policy, and mark cookies HttpOnly.
entries.more: There are three main kinds: stored (saved in the database, e.g. a comment), reflected (bounced back from a URL parameter), and DOM-based (created by client-side JavaScript). Assignment 6 on this site covers XSS security, and the Security Monitor detected 27 XSS probes like <script>alert(document.cookie)</script>.

entries.title: How multi-factor authentication (MFA) works
entries.tags: mfa 2fa multi factor two factor authentication authenticator code otp passkey
entries.answer: Multi-factor authentication requires two or more different kinds of proof before you can log in: something you know (a password), something you have (a phone authenticator app, security key, or passkey), or something you are (fingerprint or face). Even if an attacker steals your password, they still can't get in without the second factor.
entries.more: Strongest to weakest: hardware security keys and passkeys (phishing-resistant), authenticator app codes, then SMS codes (better than nothing, but vulnerable to SIM swapping). Never share an MFA code with anyone; real support staff won't ask for it. Watch out for 'MFA fatigue', where attackers spam approval prompts hoping you tap Approve.

entries.title: What to do if you suspect your computer has been hacked
entries.tags: hacked compromised breach suspect infected what to do incident response account taken over
entries.answer: If you think you've been hacked: disconnect the device from the internet; from a different, trusted device change the passwords for your email, banking, and other important accounts and turn on MFA; run a full antivirus scan; check accounts for unfamiliar logins, forwarding rules, or purchases; tell your bank if financial details may be exposed; and report it to your IT department if it's a work or school device.
entries.more: Common signs: unexpected pop-ups or new programs, the browser homepage changing, a sudden slowdown, friends receiving messages you didn't send, or login alerts you don't recognise. If problems persist after a scan, back up personal files and reinstall the operating system. Keep notes of what happened; they help investigators.

entries.title: Protecting your personal information online
entries.tags: personal information privacy protect data online identity theft share social media
entries.answer: To protect your personal information: share less on social media (birthdays, addresses, and travel plans help attackers); check privacy settings; use unique passwords and MFA; only enter details on HTTPS sites you reached yourself; avoid public Wi-Fi for sensitive tasks or use a VPN; be wary of quizzes and forms asking for personal details; and review app permissions on your phone.
entries.more: Also consider freezing your credit with the credit bureaus to block identity theft, shredding documents with personal data, and using email aliases for sign-ups. Under privacy laws you can often request that companies delete data they hold about you.

entries.title: Identifying a suspicious website
entries.tags: suspicious website fake site scam url domain https padlock shopping check legit
entries.answer: Signs of a suspicious website: a misspelled or odd domain (paypa1.com, amazon-security-check.net), no HTTPS or certificate warnings, prices that are too good to be true, pressure to act fast, poor spelling and design, no real contact information, and requests for unusual payment methods like gift cards or crypto. The padlock only means the connection is encrypted, not that the site is honest.
entries.more: Before entering details, type the address yourself or use a bookmark rather than following a link, search for reviews of the site, and use a URL checker such as Google Safe Browsing. Your password manager refusing to autofill is another strong hint that the domain is fake.

entries.title: Brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks
entries.tags: brute force credential stuffing login attempts guess password failed logins lockout
entries.answer: A brute-force attack guesses passwords over and over against one account. Credential stuffing uses username and password pairs leaked from other sites, trying them across many accounts. Defences include account lockout or increasing delays after failed attempts, CAPTCHA, MFA, and monitoring for many failures from one IP.
entries.more: The Security Monitor detected both: 380 failed logins for 'admin' from one IP (peak 93 in five minutes), and one IP trying 130 different usernames, two of which succeeded. Those two accounts need password resets, which shows why unique passwords matter.

entries.title: Intrusion detection systems (IDS)
entries.tags: intrusion detection ids ips siem monitoring logs anomaly signature alert
entries.answer: An intrusion detection system watches network traffic or logs for signs of attack and raises alerts. Signature-based IDS match known attack patterns (like SQL injection strings); anomaly-based IDS learn what normal looks like and flag deviations (like a sudden traffic spike). An intrusion prevention system (IPS) can also block the traffic. A SIEM collects logs from many systems so analysts can correlate events.
entries.more: This site's Security Monitor is a small IDS: six explainable rules over a week of web and login logs (brute force, credential stuffing, SQL injection, XSS, HTTP flood, impossible travel), feeding a threat score. Assignment 7 adds the machine-learning side, detecting DDoS flows with a Random Forest.

entries.title: The CIA triad
entries.tags: cia triad confidentiality integrity availability security goals
entries.answer: The CIA triad is the core model of information security. Confidentiality means only authorised people can read data (encryption, access control). Integrity means data isn't altered without permission (hashes, signatures). Availability means systems are up when needed (redundancy, DDoS protection, backups).
entries.more: Each attack type maps to one of these: phishing and data breaches hit confidentiality, SQL injection and XSS can hit integrity, and DoS/DDoS attacks hit availability, the focus of Assignment 7.

entries.title: Why software updates and patching matter
entries.tags: update patch software vulnerability zero day exploit outdated
entries.answer: Updates fix security vulnerabilities that attackers actively exploit. Turn on automatic updates for your operating system, browser, and apps, and replace devices that no longer receive updates. A zero-day is a flaw attackers use before a patch exists, which is why defence in depth (MFA, backups, least privilege) still matters.

entries.title: Public Wi-Fi and VPNs
entries.tags: public wifi wi-fi vpn coffee shop hotspot network safe encrypt
entries.answer: Public Wi-Fi can be monitored or impersonated by a fake hotspot. Prefer HTTPS sites, avoid banking or entering passwords on open networks, turn off auto-join, and use your phone's hotspot or a reputable VPN, which encrypts traffic between your device and the VPN provider.

entries.title: Social engineering
entries.tags: social engineering manipulation pretexting impersonation tailgating human
entries.answer: Social engineering manipulates people rather than technology: pretending to be IT support, a boss, or a delivery company to get passwords, codes, or access. Slow down, verify requests through a separate channel you trust, and never share passwords or MFA codes.

entries.title: Encryption and HTTPS
entries.tags: encryption https tls ssl certificate padlock encrypt data
entries.answer: Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the right key can read it. HTTPS uses TLS to encrypt traffic between your browser and a website, protecting passwords and data from eavesdroppers. It proves you're connected to the domain shown, but not that the site's owner is trustworthy.

entries.title: Lab 1: Identity and security (ipconfig, ping, tracert, ARP)
entries.tags: lab 1 ipconfig ping tracert arp mac address ip address subnet mask dhcp ttl network identity
entries.answer: Lab 1 (CPS 3498) explored a Windows computer's network identity. ipconfig /all shows the IP address, subnet mask, gateway, MAC address, and DNS servers, and ipconfig /renew gets a new address from DHCP. ping to the gateway measured about 2 ms with TTL 64 (the hop limit that stops packets looping forever). tracert mapped the route to kean.edu and google.com (about 8 hops), and arp -a listed IP-to-MAC mappings.
entries.more: Security relevance: knowing your IP and MAC identity is the basis for spotting spoofing. ARP has no authentication, so ARP spoofing lets an attacker on the same network intercept traffic, and tracert and ping help diagnose whether a site is down because of an attack or a network fault.

entries.title: Assignment 8: Intrusion detection and an AI assistant that controls the website
entries.tags: assignment 8 chatbot assistant digital human voice commands control website intrusion detection
entries.answer: Assignment 8 adds two things. First, the Security Monitor dashboard analyses a week of web and login logs for brute force, credential stuffing, SQL injection, XSS, an HTTP flood, and impossible travel, and rates the threat level. Second, it adds me, Shield: an assistant you can type or speak to that changes the site's appearance, plays music or the training video, navigates pages, and answers security questions.
entries.more: I only run a fixed whitelist of website actions: I can't access your files, other apps, or your operating system, and I don't store what you say. Voice uses your browser's built-in speech recognition. Answers come from a curated knowledge base, plus Gemini when the site has an API key configured.

entries.title: How the assignments relate to the overall project
entries.tags: assignments relate overall project relationship connect all assignments 1 2 3 4 5 9 course
entries.answer: Everything builds on one site, SpamShield AI. Lab 1 covers network identity (IP, MAC, ARP). Assignment 6 set out the research method for machine-learning spam detection and covered XSS security. The main project trains ten models to detect SMS spam and phishing. Assignment 7 applies the same data-driven approach to DDoS detection and website availability. Assignment 8 adds a security monitoring dashboard and this assistant.
entries.more: Documents for the other course assignments haven't been added to the site yet, so I can only answer about the ones listed in the Assignments tab. The common thread is using data and machine learning to detect attacks (spam, phishing, DDoS, intrusions) while explaining the results clearly.

entries.title: SpamShield AI project and Assignment 6 spam detection results
entries.tags: spamshield project spam detection sms machine learning model accuracy assignment 6 research method random forest logistic regression results
entries.answer: SpamShield AI detects SMS spam and phishing with machine learning. It uses the Kaggle SMS Spam Collection (5,572 messages, 13.4% spam), TF-IDF text features plus engineered signals like URLs and money symbols, and compares ten models. The top-ranked model, XGBoost, reached 98.94% accuracy and 95.62% F1, against the Logistic Regression baseline at 98.55% accuracy and 94.30% F1. Assignment 6 defined this research method.
entries.more: You can paste any message into the Live Detector to see the prediction, confidence, and which words drove it. Precision matters because false positives block real messages; recall matters because false negatives let scams through.

entries.title: Assignment 7: DoS/DDoS attacks and website availability
entries.tags: assignment 7 ddos cic-ids2017 dataset website availability traffic detection movie
entries.answer: Assignment 7 analysed 225,745 network flows from CIC-IDS2017's Friday DDoS capture. Attack flows all targeted port 80 and were individually small and slow, so a volume threshold scored only 0.03% F1. A Random Forest on flow-shape features reached 99.96% F1 with 0 false alarms and 5 missed attacks. It also includes an AI-generated movie about restoring website availability.
entries.more: Takeaway: detect DDoS by combining per-flow classification with aggregate rate monitoring. Limits: one capture, one attack tool (LOIC), lab traffic, and classifying flows without time windows.

entries.title: Security Monitor dashboard results
entries.tags: security monitor dashboard threat level failed logins suspicious ip detected attacks logs events
entries.answer: The Security Monitor analysed 18,800 log events over 7 days: 2,395 login attempts (618 failed), 95 suspicious IPs, and 6 detected attacks. The threat level is Severe (100/100). Incidents: Brute-force login (high); Impossible travel (high); SQL injection probe (high); Credential stuffing (critical); Cross-site scripting (XSS) probe (medium); HTTP flood (DDoS) (critical).
entries.more: Normal vs suspicious: normal IPs average 1.7 events per active hour with a 5.8% login failure rate; suspicious IPs average 91.5 with 99.4% failures. The log is synthetic with planted incidents, so no real system was attacked.
